### 1. Traditional reading

**vv. 23–30 (overview):** Guzik titles this section "the command to praise the LORD." He says God's own people have a special duty to praise Him, but the whole earth is also called to announce His salvation every day. (EW)

**v. 23:** Guzik quotes Spurgeon: every person has reason to sing, and every believer especially ought to praise the Lord's name. (EW)

**v. 24:** Guzik reads this as David speaking to God's people again, urging them to tell everyone how great God is and that He is above all gods. (EW)

**vv. 25–26:** Guzik says God is greater because the other nations' gods are only idols, while the LORD made the heavens. Israel's covenant God is real and created everything; the nations have only statues. (EW)

**v. 27:** The Biblical Illustrator preaches on "strength and gladness" in God's dwelling. Its points are that Christ's grace frees us from worry about the future, and that we find lasting strength and gladness when we remember we are doing God's will in all we do or endure. (BI)

**vv. 28–29:** The Biblical Illustrator says these verses explain why we gather in God's house: to worship, not just to listen. It argues this condemns people who stay away saying "I can read my Bible at home." That excuse might work for someone who only comes to hear, but not for a worshipper. (BI)

**vv. 31–33:**
- Guzik says David knew creation itself praises God. Its beauty, power, skill and majesty are a witness to its Creator. (EW)
- Guzik cites the scholar Payne, who suggests the line "He is coming to judge the earth" may be the first place in written Scripture to teach Christ's glorious second coming. (EW)

**v. 34:**
- The Preacher's Homiletical Commentary lists the themes as thanks for God's goodness, and mercy that reaches the miserable, lasts forever and outweighs sin and rebellion. (PHC)
- A Pulpit Commentary homily (J.R. Thomson) says congregations don't need less prayer but do need more praise. Since God's mercy lasts forever, praise of Him should never stop. (PC)

**v. 35:** Matthew Henry says that when we rejoice in God's blessings we should remember fellow believers who are scattered or oppressed, and pray for their rescue as if it were our own. Believers belong to one another, so "save us" is a fitting way to pray "save them." (MH)

**v. 36:**
- Guzik says the people's shared "Amen" shows the psalm wasn't a solo performance. It expressed the whole community's agreement and praise. (EW)
- The Preacher's Homiletical Commentary says praise should be continual: God has been blessed from eternity and will be through eternity, so He should be praised without pause. (PHC)

**v. 37:**
- Henry says worshipping God shouldn't be limited to the occasional grand celebration; it should be daily work. That is why David set up a fixed routine for those serving at each post. (MH)
- The Preacher's Homiletical Commentary calls this a "perpetual service": a permanent ministry and regular choir in a fixed place and proper order. (PHC)

**vv. 39–40:**
- Henry notes that in Moses' tabernacle and later in Solomon's temple, the ark and the altar stood together. From Eli's time until the temple was built, they were apart. He says he can't work out why David, who knew the Law, didn't reunite them. (MH)
- Henry says the sacrifices had to continue. By nature they ranked below prayer and praise, but they pictured in advance ("types") Christ's work as go-between for God and people, so keeping them up mattered a great deal. (MH)
- Precept Austin gives the text of v. 40, but the excerpt had no comment on it. (PA)

**v. 41:**
- Henry notes that David also put singers at Gibeon, where the altar was. The theme of all their songs was "His mercy endures forever." (MH)
- Precept Austin heads this verse "thank the Lord for His everlasting lovingkindness." It notes the Hebrew word for "give thanks" is *yadah* (the Greek Old Testament uses *aineo*). (PA)

**Not covered by what I could read:** vv. 30, 32 on its own, 38, 42 and 43.
